Hence, the strategy employed was to investigate commonly available practical alloys with reasonably high chromium (Cr) content such as austenitic 300 series stainless steel. To mitigate the susceptibility of austenitic stainless steel (SS) to intergranular corrosion due to sensitization — lowered chromium content due to chromium carbide precipitation at the grain boundaries— that is likely to occur near the weld area during welding and stress relief annealing, stainless steel with carbon content less than a maximum of 0.03% (denoted by suffix ‘L’) [27] are preferred. Based on the above information and with feedback from the experts identified in Task 1, the following samples listed in Table 2 were selected for the corrosion and mechanical durability studies. Despite aluminum’s low strength at high temperatures, aluminum alloy was also investigated because its high sulfidation resistance and high thermal conductivity provides compelling argument to use them as heat transfer enhancement structures in the form of fins, for which strength bearing properties is not a major concern. A total of 40 flat coupons, 8 each for SS-316L, SS-317L, SS-347, Corten B and Al 5052 were first tested. Multiple samples of the same material were investigated as necessary so that they can be removed at different intervals during the testing process to estimate the corrosion rates and kinetics. Based on the results, SS-347 and Corten-B were eliminated due to high cost and high corrosion rate, respectively, for the next set of corrosion studies with welded and stressed-welded (U-bend) coupons. A total of 40 coupons 7 straight-welded and 3 stressed-welded coupons each for SS-316L, SS-317L, SS-304 and SA516-70 were tested in the second round.
